questions.q: What kind of backup do mongodump and mongorestore perform?
options: A logical backup — data is captured and rebuilt document by document, not as a raw copy of storage files
A physical backup that copies raw data files byte-for-byte
An in-memory-only backup that cannot be persisted to disk
A backup that only works on MongoDB Atlas
questions.explain: mongodump/mongorestore operate at the logical document level, reading data out and rebuilding it on restore, unlike a raw file copy.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff of using mongodump on a large production deployment?
options: It's slower than a physical snapshot at scale and adds load to the running server while it executes
It cannot back up more than one collection at a time
It only works if authentication is disabled
It permanently locks the database until the backup finishes
questions.explain: Reading and rewriting every document is slower than copying raw files and adds resource load to the running server, a real limitation at scale.

questions.q: What must be true for a filesystem snapshot backup to be consistent and restorable?
options: Writes are locked during the snapshot (or, more commonly, the snapshot is taken against a secondary with journaling enabled)
Nothing extra is required — any snapshot at any time is automatically consistent
The database must be running on Atlas
Authentication must be disabled during the snapshot
questions.explain: A consistent snapshot requires either locking writes with fsyncLock or snapshotting a journaled secondary so the primary is undisturbed.

questions.q: What does Atlas continuous backup provide that a self-managed backup script doesn't handle automatically?
options: Continuous change capture via the oplog enabling point-in-time restore, with no manual scripting or orchestration
It removes the need for any backup at all, since Atlas never loses data
It only supports full-cluster backups, never point-in-time restore
It requires the same manual mongodump scheduling as self-managed deployments
questions.explain: Atlas continuous backup captures changes via the oplog for point-in-time restore, without a self-maintained backup pipeline.

questions.q: Which of these is a real advantage of mongodump over a filesystem snapshot?
options: It can flexibly target a single database or collection, and works across different MongoDB versions and storage engines
It is always faster than a filesystem snapshot regardless of data size
It requires no server resources while running
It automatically enables point-in-time restore like Atlas
questions.explain: Because it works at the logical level, mongodump is flexible about scope and portable across versions/engines, unlike a raw file snapshot.
